thread_title: S. flava Bulloch Co, GA (recently extirpated site)
breadcrumb: S. flava Bulloch Co, GA (recently extirpated site)

posts.body_html:
I say with great optimism that many sites in the wild will likely live on, since if you think about it, they still exist today and have gone through great abuse. I also said in many other posts that I had a gut feeling that some of these sites will no longer be in the future.


In most cases, who really knows? My gut told me this site in Bulloch Co, GA would live on for our great, great, great, great grandchildren to see and enjoy, since it was located in a seemingly protected zone under a powerline. Afterall, how can you develop under a powerline, it's an easement on the parcel map that can't be developed, right?

Sadly, those easement laws that apply here in California have no merit in Georgia. Yup, somehow they built houses under a powerline, and to add insult to injury, this happened in 2012! Yes, even in very recent times, we are still losing habitat despite the fact that these once common plants that you could see for miles and miles are now incredibly scarce and threatened in the wild.

I do commend the organizations that came about and rescued these plants before the site was destroyed. This is one of the rare situations where digging up plants is justified (I think 95% of the time, it isn't justified). I've heard recent reports that the plants are thriving at Atlanta Botanical Gardens, Georgia Southern University, and I have a small population as well. However, you can't replace wild populations...we may have saved most of the Sarracenia flavas at this site, but every last other plant and animal species that was there is now gone forever. There also used to be S. minor and S. psittacina in the area, but I'm not sure if those still exist.

What's even more heart breaking is that I've now heard conflicting reports on where the black veined flava originated (previously, I heard reports that it came from the Kennedy tract, which is nearby). This powercut may in fact have been the spot where our coveted black veined flava originated.

The water table was already destroyed by bulldozing the forest, so even if they left all the plants there, they would have dried up and died long ago.


These pictures are from Georgia Wildlife Rescue. If you are the owner of these photos and would like to have them removed, please contact me: meizzwang@gmail.com



These photos were taken Aug. 2012. In the background, where you see bull dozers, there are now homes and a few shops. Prior to this photo being taken, the whole surrounding area used to be thick forest with native plants (I remember finding some native persimmons there):

posts.body_html:
Calen: I refained from selfing these babies because in case you didn't know, it took over a decade for those original black veined flavas to bloom (they were the result of selfing). Instead, to help increase vigor, I crossed one of my best pure black veined plants from Bulloch Co with a plant from the population above that was vigorous and showed decent venation.

Rhizomatous, If I was a politician, I'd have an answer for you. I think there are still a lot of conservationists in general haven't bought into the idea of reintroductions, but over time, I believe they will realize it's the best thing we can do for these plants. The challenge is finding the right location, ensuring stock plants are true to location, weed/disease/pest free, and making sure the new location is managed/monitored in the long run.

posts.body_html:
for comparison, here are some black veined flavas from bulloch co, GA. These traps just opened, so the veins aren't yet black, that happens as the pitchers age. Notice in the first picture below, the red line in the throat:


pitcher just about to open:






Even with a somewhat pronounced red throat, you can still see the red line:

It's tough to see, but I can attest that those rescued plants were re-homed at some great facilities and are still thriving. I know a few of the folks who coordinated that rescue.

As for reintroduction, it has been successful and is working very well. Conservationists have gotten extremely good at locating potential reintroduction sites, especially with GIS technologies, hydrological mapping, etc.

However, I would prioritize in-situ conservation at any cost. Before too long, we'll have destroyed so many habitats and potential habitats that there simply won't be anywhere left to reintroduce plants. These habitats are so fragile, with so many parameters that need to be just right. That only comes once in a blue moon, especially for mountain bogs. 

While reintroduction is definitely a good tool, I would hate for lawmakers to start saying "so what if developers destroy pitcherplant habitat--can't they just move em?" Most of the public does not and possibly will not ever understand how crucial it is to preserve the populations that are thriving.

posts.body_html: The law in Georgia states that you can essentially do anything you want with any plants on your property, even if they are state-protected or federally endangered. ESA and state laws only apply to public land. The few private landowners who work with the DNR and FWS to preserve rare plants are truly awesome people, and their contributions might generally go unnoticed.

posts.body_html:
Here in California, before any buildings are in place, a building permit is required (this can take years to get). During the process, it's not uncommon to have a public hearing, and if the neighbors attend and there is enough support, they can stop you from building. If the County doesn't like your plans for any reason whatsoever, they can stop you from building as well. Trees of certain sizes cannot be cut down, but regretfully, fields filled with rare flowers can be destroyed. On pristine habitat, I'm all for this sort of restriction, but for properties that are already fully destroyed, it seems like governmental over-reach.

I had a friend who recently built a home on a lot where there was an endangered grass. They were required to seed their property with the endangered grass, but the seeds came from another state! Great intentions, bad policies.....

On one hand, I'm all about freedom and having rights (within reason) to do what you want with your land. On the other hand, you can see that people's freedom has resulted in the extinction of many unique, pristine habitats in many states....most people don't care, but for those of us who do, it's pretty insulting and irresponsible to see this continue.
